prompt: Write an essay on whether people learn more from failure or from success.
text:
# Do We Learn More from Failure or from Success?

The proverb says we learn from our mistakes. The success literature says we should study winners. Both claims have merit, but they describe different kinds of learning. Failure teaches more efficiently and more deeply about what does not work, while success teaches best when it is examined as critically as failure usually is. The real question is not which experience contains more information, but which one we are more likely to extract it from.

## The Case for Failure

Failure's first advantage is that it is hard to ignore. When a plan collapses, an exam goes badly, or a product flops, the gap between expectation and reality is stark. Psychologists have long observed that surprise drives learning: when outcomes match predictions, there is little reason to update our mental models, but when they do not, we are forced to revise them. Failure is, almost by definition, a prediction error.

Second, failure tends to provoke analysis. After a loss, people ask why. Aviation and medicine, fields in which errors are costly, have built institutions around this instinct: incident investigations, black-box recorders, and morbidity and mortality conferences. The remarkable safety record of modern commercial aviation owes much to the systematic study of crashes. Each failure becomes a lesson that benefits an entire industry.

Third, failure builds traits that success cannot easily supply: resilience, humility, and an accurate sense of one's limits. A person who has never failed has never tested their ability to recover. Those who have been through setbacks often report that the experience clarified their priorities and exposed assumptions they did not know they held.

## The Case for Success

Yet failure has real limits as a teacher. A single failure is often ambiguous. Did the startup fail because of the product, the timing, the team, or plain bad luck? Because failures usually have many possible causes, people frequently draw the wrong conclusion, blaming external circumstances or, conversely, over-blaming themselves. Failure also tells us what did not work without showing what will. There are endless ways to do something wrong, and eliminating them one at a time is slow.

Success, by contrast, provides a positive example. It confirms that a set of actions, under certain conditions, can produce a desired result. Learning a language, mastering an instrument, or building a business requires not just avoiding errors but accumulating correct practice. Skills are consolidated through successful repetition, and confidence gained from early wins sustains the motivation needed to continue. Research on learning suggests that a high rate of success, with challenge at the edge of ability, often produces faster progress than constant struggle, because discouraged learners quit.

Success also reveals things failure cannot: which strengths to build on, which strategies scale, and what effective execution actually looks like.

## The Problem of Interpretation

The trouble is that neither experience teaches automatically. Success is vulnerable to a well-known bias: we attribute it to skill and attribute failure to bad luck. This self-serving bias means that success often teaches nothing, or teaches false lessons. A trader who profits in a rising market may conclude he is brilliant. A company that thrives may copy habits that were irrelevant to its fortune. Worse, studying only successful cases produces survivorship bias: we see the entrepreneurs who took big risks and won, and forget the many who took the same risks and lost.

Failure suffers from the opposite distortion. People may avoid reflecting on it because it is painful, or they may overgeneralize ("I'm just bad at this"), drawing demoralizing conclusions that block further learning. Research on motivation suggests that the effect of failure depends heavily on mindset: those who see ability as improvable treat failure as information, while those who see it as fixed treat it as a verdict.

So the quality of learning depends less on the outcome than on the reflection that follows. A failure ignored teaches nothing; a success carefully dissected can teach a great deal.

## A Synthesis

If forced to choose, I would say that failure teaches more per event, because it jolts us into scrutiny and exposes flawed assumptions that success leaves hidden. But the most reliable learning comes from combining both: using success to learn what to do and failure to learn what to avoid and why. Beginners benefit especially from early success to build competence and motivation; experts, who succeed often, benefit especially from failure at the edge of their abilities, where the lessons are subtle.

The best learners, then, treat both outcomes with the same skepticism. After a failure they ask, "What did I actually control, and what would I change?" After a success they ask, "What role did luck play, and would this work again?" Done honestly, this turns every outcome into information.

## Conclusion

Failure is the more forceful teacher, and success the more encouraging one. Failure corrects our errors; success shows us what is possible. People learn the most not from either one alone but from the willingness to examine both without flattery or despair. In the end, outcomes supply the raw material, and reflection does the teaching.
